en: Along the dark plain,
Taitoru was coming.
When she looked carefully through the telescope,
He was behind thirty wondrous steeds.
'Oh, my dear swift steed,
You were a renowned racehorse.
I tell my anguish to God!
Dear creature, you had sixty years of maturity.
Do not let my words grow cold.
Do not make them call me a crazed woman
And bring disgrace upon me.
Do not make me wail any longer,
O one Almighty Creator,
Do not make my eyes weep.
Do not make my words come to nothing,
Do not shame me.'
Protesting as she said this,
Upon the saddle-shaped ridge,
Your luckless sister-in-law,
Unable to stand grieving and weeping,
Wishing to die yet unable to die,
Unable to cut short her surviving life,
Her thoughts painfully divided,
As though stricken with wasting sickness,
The tears streamed from your mother's eyes.
Her poor heart would not grow still,
Was torn apart so many times.
The poor soul stood lamenting
On the plain where no crow flew.
Her grief and fear were
Of the child born from her womb,
Of her spring feeding a valley river.
The poor soul feared especially
That orphan born of herself.
Once more your unfortunate sister-in-law,
The poor woman built like a warrior,
Now gathered her senses.
Turning back, struggling,
Imploring the one God,
She looked through the telescope again.
Again observing her bay horse,
Again she learned his condition.
At the mist-covered spur,
At the headland of the gray hills,
Upon the ridge of Kezenche,
Taitoru was coming
Along broad Ak-Chiy.
'Again my swift steed is coming.'
He was behind twelve wondrous steeds then.
Her heart was torn apart,
Unable to stand and watch,
The tears streamed from your mother's eyes.
With golden forelock and tasseled belt,
Azyz Khan's only son,
The swift steed Taitoru,
Upon the bright horse Sarala,
Your Alake seemed to be driving forward.
Wearing yellow leather trousers,
Bearing a spear without a tassel,
A bare sword fastened at his side,
His sturdy waist girded,
When he saw seventy thousand troops,
He swept in and attacked,
Not a hair recoiling from death,
Never drawing back from dying.
Your champion with a guardian's support,
My champion, the son of light,
Had received a letter from Khan Kozho,
Had received the caliph's blessing.
That dear lion, born surpassing others,
Was also named the mighty conquering champion.
His amassed wealth was left in Kakan;
What he most desired was religion and faith.
His amassed wealth was left in Beijing;
What he cherished was faith.
The religions he chose and knew,
The caliph and sultan spiritual guides,
The religions he esteemed and knew,
The sultan spiritual guides in Mecca—
The true religion entered his dream,
Purity entered his heart.
Because of the Last Judgment,
Because that damned Hell exists,
Because of the next world,
Because a tormenting Hell exists,
He was cleansed of the dark religion,
Fled the unbelievers and became a stranger,
Scattered the wealth he had amassed,
Desired only faith.
Shrouding himself in the dark day,
His father the khan, Azyz Khan,
He implored, 'Become a Muslim.'
When his appeals would not bring him to the faith,
When he would not heed his words,
He cast away his golden throne.
His father Azyz Khan
He killed in Great Beijing.
He bloodied his silver throne,
Killed his father Kun Zhang-Zhung.
The holy man seen in his sleep,
Paradise and Hell seen in his dream—
For this wretched life of suffering,
He witnessed a most wondrous thing.
Surviving because he had not died,
When he had newly become a Muslim,
He took the warrior Mazhik along,
Made Altynai his companion.
His good days gone, he was oppressed.
From the forty thieving Chinese unbelievers,
The Muslim who gathered the forty companions at his death.
The steel spear in his hand
He held and thrust without wavering.
With cotton belt and broad boots,
The monks' khan Konurbai
Fought him without pause for six months.
'That great idol made of bronze,
Calling it God,
How can I stand muttering before it?
From turbulent Hell
I shall free my soul,' he said.
'The faith I cherish is pure;
I shall reach Mecca and settle there,' he said.
'That great idol made of bronze,
Calling it God,' he said,
"How could I be an unbeliever?" he said.
He fought fiercely for six months;
He was struck from the flank.
His mother Altynay,
These men and his forty companions—
He lost them to China as spoils.
Drenched in bloody gore,
He fought alone without fleeing.
Purified of the dark faith,
He fled the unbelievers and became a stranger.
He came and settled in Talas,
Became a friend till Judgment Day,
And served as a companion to Manas.
Holding his spear, he broke through the ranks;
He entered Kakan's land and fell to a bullet.
Upon the horse Aysarala,
A racer like Taytoru—
"My dear friend's horse!" he said.
Dear Almambet rode urging it on.
On this side of him—
Much is false, much is true.
This lion, the renowned conqueror—
No one has come back from seeing him.
Half is false, half is true;
No one has returned from his side.
Tall of body, broad of shoulder,
The most skillful of spearmen,
The finest of the tawny-faced men,
The noblest of heroes,
The best of the forty companions,
Among Manas's spearmen,
The skillful one who shook the world:
Chubak, son of Khan Baltay,
With piercing cries and shrill battle shouts.
No man's strength could match him in a fight;
A lion's teeth could not pierce him.
He wore a coat of blue rep cloth,
Rode a horse such as Kökala.
Your Chubak, son of the unseen world,
Your lad who knew no sorrow.
How many lands he threw into turmoil,
That furious lad of yours!
His bulk matched a mountain;
He seemed ready to devour whoever appeared.
A banner could be seen in his hand;
Venom poured from his mouth.
When he shouted and thrust his spear,
He seemed an army of forty thousand.
When he roared and thrust his spear,
Many men, thrown into confusion,
Scattered in every direction.
Chubak, son of Lord Baltay,
Your warrior, Manas's mighty champion—
At that time, the lion Chubak
Had died in Beijing.
The one to bind at his waist,
Valiant Manas's mighty champion.
Almambet and Chubak were heroes,
All twelve parts of their bodies in perfect balance,
Heroes who shook the world.
Khan Manas's Akkula,
Khan Chubak's Kökala,
Almambet's Sarala,
Khan Bakai's Köktulpar,
Warrior Syrgak's Kökchebich—
Untrodden by these noble steeds,
No whole tract of land remained.
Without having heard their battle cry,
No whole people remained.
Almambet and Chubak, the paired heroes,
Raised their shouts.
Those champions who had died as martyrs,
"My dear friend's horse!" they said,
Urged it on all the harder.
If you look toward the front,
His blade of dark steel—
Have you heard of him?
Khan Manas's Syrgak.
He never rested on his elbow,
Never took even a wink of sleep.
Light in the saddle, watchful on the road,
The sleepless warrior Syrgak
Had strength to match the world.
Manas and this Syrgak
Were the sons of brothers.
His sword rested in its sheath;
When he attacked an eager foe,
He too drenched him in red blood.
He never followed wicked counsel,
Never slunk away from an enemy.
Who rode a splendid courser,
He wore a coat of blue iron,
The finest of the sixty,
The precious one among forty companions,
Worth them all.
Young Syrgak, the outstanding hero,
With piercing cries and resounding battle shouts,
Raised his voice without restraint.
The dear lion who died a martyr—
Fallen in the flower of his days,
Dear young Syrgak, whose death brought grief,
Was himself urging the horse on.
The great lead rope tied in knotted loops,
Dear Syrgak drew from his hand
And struck the horse's flank.
Dear Syrgak urged it on.
If you look behind him,
His face like oiled wheat,
His eyes like twilight mist,
A black-spotted leopard
Charging at his side,
A maimed, fierce lion
Moving beside him, ready—
The leopard of peerless fortune,
Who brought hardship upon this poor head,
My saint who went to the other world,
Who made the broad world narrow,
Who left me yearning for one glimpse.
When he launched a campaign against Kakan,
He led the army of Islam.
At thirty-two,
He left his unfortunate one bereft.
United when they were tiny as lice,
Joined when they were small as thumbs,
Her sovereign, Khan Manas,
"My poor dear one's horse!" he said,
And himself galloped after it.
The two khans, Ajybay and Bakai,
"Our poor dear friend's horse!" they said,
And galloped after it too.
Your noble mother Kanykei,
Dividing the hair down her back in ten,
